extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and practitioners of English common law and property/political-constitutional history
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes rules and doctrines governing royal revenue and incident property rights (demesnes, prerogatives, wrecks, treasure, forfeitures, deodands, escheats, custody of idiots) in historic English common law as explained in Blackstone's Commentaries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on crown grants and leases (demesne lands)
rubrics_metrics.description: All future grants or leases from the crown for any longer term than thirty one years or three lives are declared to be void; except with regard to houses, which may be granted for fifty years. And no reversionary lease can be made, so as to exceed, together with the estate in being, the same term of three lives or thirty one years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where there is a subsisting lease, the king cannot grant a future interest that would make the combined term exceed 31 years or three lives (example: if a subsisting lease has 20 years left, the king cannot grant a future interest longer than 11 years). Tenants under such grants must be made liable for committing waste, and the usual rent must be reserved, or where there has been no rent, one third of the clear yearly value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prerogative of purveyance and pre-emption (historical scope and abolition)
rubrics_metrics.description: The crown enjoyed a right of buying provisions and other necessaries by purveyors at appraised valuation in preference to others, and could forcibly impress carriages and horses for royal business.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This power arose when royal households were provisioned by renders rather than ready money; purveyors abused the authority, became oppressive, and the prerogative declined and was resigned at the Restoration. The statute history and foreign examples show decline/abolition (e.g., Sweden under Gustavus Adolphus). Parliament compensated the crown in part by settling hereditary excise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hereditary excise as recompense for lost prerogatives
rubrics_metrics.description: Parliament settled on the sovereign, his heirs and successors, for ever, the hereditary excise of fifteen pence per barrel on all beer and ale sold in the kingdom, and proportionable sums for certain other liquors, as part-recompense for relinquished prerogatives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This excise forms a distinct branch of the king's ordinary revenue; its nature and later implications are to be further explained elsewhere in the commentary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Revenue from wine licences (statutory changes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Wine licences and rents payable to the crown by persons licensed to sell wine retail were settled on the crown by statute (12 Car. II c.25) to compensate for abolished prerogatives, but were later abolished (30 Geo. II c.19) and replaced by an annual sum charged on stamp duties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows how statutory reform reallocated revenue sources to compensate the crown for lost feudal/prerogative incomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits from royal forests
rubrics_metrics.description: Profits arise principally in amercements or fines levied for offences against forest laws; forests have special laws, privileges, courts and officers for preservation of game and royal recreation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although historically significant, forest courts for levying amercements had been largely disused since 1632; practical importance declined though the legal structures remain to be explained in subsequent books.

rubrics_metrics.name: Profits from ordinary courts of justice and limits on grants
rubrics_metrics.description: The king's revenue included fines, forfeitures, amercements, and fees due for legal matters (setting the great seal, original writs, permits for fines to bar entails, etc.). Many of these have been granted out to private persons, or appropriated to uses; future grants by statute (1 Ann. st. 2. c. 7.) are limited to endure for no longer time than the life of the prince who grants them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These fees were originally royal perquisites as recompense for intervention; statutory limits restrict the duration of grants so as to preserve some royal interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal fish (whale and sturgeon) as crown property
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal fish (whale and sturgeon) are the king's property when thrown ashore or caught near the coasts; the right is claimed by statute de praerogativa regis and is anciently recognized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The doctrine has historical antecedents in Denmark and Normandy; treatises distinguish whale and sturgeon in some particulars.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wrecks as royal revenue and the definition of legal wreck
rubrics_metrics.description: Wrecks are declared the king's property by statute (17 Edw. II. c. 11.) and by common law; but to be legal wreck, goods must come to land—goods remaining at sea are treated as jetsam, flotsam, or ligan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ancient law harshly adjudged all goods of a lost ship to the king, but successive charters and statutes (Henry I, Henry II, Richard I, stat. Westm. 1) introduced humane rules: if any person escaped alive or goods can be identified, the owner may reclaim within statutory periods; a sheriff must keep goods for a year and a day to allow claimants to prove title; perishable goods may be sold with money held in place of goods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinctions and rules for jetsam, flotsam, and ligan
rubrics_metrics.description: Jetsam: goods cast into the sea and sink; flotsam: goods floating on the surface; ligan: goods sunk but tied to a buoy to be recovered. These remain royal if no owner appears, but the owner can recover them if he proves title.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Items cast overboard to lighten ship do not necessarily show abandonment; ligan indicates intent to recover and so is treated as retained property. Grants of wrecks do not generally pass jetsam/flotsam/ligan.

rubrics_metrics.name: Salvage, obligation to assist ships, and penalties for plundering
rubrics_metrics.description: If a ship is lost on shore (not legal wreck), goods shall be delivered to merchants on payment of a reasonable reward to rescuers (salvage). Statutes (2 Edw. III c.13; 12 Ann st. 2 c.18; 4 Geo. I c.12; 26 Geo. II c.19) impose duties on coastal officers and towns to assist ships in distress, set salvage assessment procedures, and declare plundering, obstructing rescue, false lights, and similar acts to be felonies or penal offences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Secreting goods leads to treble forfeiture; wilful acts causing ship loss (holes, stealing pumps) are felony without benefit of clergy; later statutes harshly punish plundering and deceitful seamarks and protect distressed mariners and their property.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treasure-trove (thesaurus inventus) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Hidden treasure (money, coin, plate, bullion hidden in the earth or private place with unknown owner) belongs to the king; if the hider is known or later found, the owner is entitled. Treasure found on the sea or upon the surface belongs to the finder if no owner appears.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The legal distinction hinges on 'hiding' versus 'abandoning'—hidden deposits imply intent to reclaim and thus, if owner dies and secret dies with him, the treasure becomes royal. Historically, medieval and Roman laws varied; penalties for concealing hidden treasure from the king once were severe, though later reduced to fines and imprisonment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Waifs (bona waviata) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Waifs are goods stolen and thrown away by a thief in his flight; these are given to the king by law as punishment on the owner for not pursuing the felon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the robbed party promptly pursues (makes fresh suit), convicts the thief, or procures evidence, he shall recover his goods. Waived goods do not belong to the king until seized for his use; if the party robbed seizes them first, the king cannot later claim them. Goods hidden by the thief (not thrown away in flight) are not waifs. The goods of a foreign merchant shall never be waifs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estrays (found domestic animals) rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Estrays are tame or reclaimable valuable animals found wandering with no known owner; by proclamation in church and two neighbouring market towns and after a year and a day with no claim, they vest in the king or his grantee (often the lord of the manor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the owner claims within the year he must pay costs of finding, keeping, and proclaiming. Only animals with recoverable property value (cattle, swans—royal fowl) qualify; ferae naturae and animals without legal value (e.g., some dogs/cats) do not. The taker must keep and feed the estray and may not use it as labour (may milk for preservation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Bona vacantia principle
rubrics_metrics.description: Goods in which no one else can claim property (bona vacantia) belong to the sovereign; the law shifts property that in nature belonged to the first occupant to the prince by positive law to avoid disputes and to support the public authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This supplies a unifying rationale for royal fish, wrecks, treasure-trove, waifs, and estrays; cited as deriving from natural law and becoming 'jus gentium' in practice among modern states.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forfeitures for offences (bona confiscata)
rubrics_metrics.description: Forfeitures of lands and goods for offences (bona confiscata or forisfacta) vest in the king; the substantial ground for forfeiture is that property is derived from society and violating the social compact forfeits the offender's civil rights to such property.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Severity varies by offence—atrocious offences can produce total confiscation of moveables and perpetual or temporary loss of real estate. The particulars are addressed under the law of crimes; general doctrine explained here as part of the royal revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deodand (forfeiture of chattel causing death)
rubrics_metrics.description: A deodand is any personal chattel that is the immediate occasion of the death of a reasonable creature; it is forfeited to the king to be applied to pious uses. Things in motion that cause death (animals, carts) are forfeited more fully than stationary objects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No deodand where an infant under years of discretion is killed by a fall from a thing standing still (linked to theological notions of sin/atonement); if an animal in motion kills (infant or adult) it is forfeited. If an instrument caused death (e.g., sword used by another), the instrument is a deodand. Instruments and values are presented by a grand jury in homicide indictments for potential claim. No deodands due for accidents on the high sea (outside common law jurisdiction), though drowning in fresh water may implicate vessel and cargo.

rubrics_metrics.name: Royal mines (gold and silver) and statutory limits on royal claim
rubrics_metrics.description: Royal mines originally derived from coinage prerogative; the king is entitled to gold and silver found in mines. By statutes (1 W. & M. st. 1. c. 30 and 5 W. & M. c. 6) mines of copper, tin, iron, or lead shall not be royal mines even if gold or silver is extracted; the crown may take the precious metal paying a price equal to the base metal value (except tin in Devon/Cornwall).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Statutory change encouraged private mining by preventing private owners' discouragement at the risk of royal claim, while preserving a limited royal interest (payment for precious metal in base-metal mines).

rubrics_metrics.name: Escheats (reversion to crown on defect of heirs)
rubrics_metrics.description: Escheats of lands happen upon defect of heirs to the inheritance and in general revert to and vest in the king, who is deemed original proprietor of all lands in the kingdom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes this branch of revenue is properly treated in the second book (acquisition and loss of land by escheat) and is mentioned here for regularity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Custody of idiots (wardship of natural fools) and attendant profits
rubrics_metrics.description: An idiot (natural fool with no understanding from nativity) is by law presumed never likely to attain understanding; custody of him and his lands was vested in the lord of the fee but, due to abuses, was provided to the king (statute 17 Edw. II. c. 9.) who takes the profits without waste and must find necessaries, rendering the estate to heirs after death.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: There is a writ de idiota inquirendo tried by a jury of twelve to determine status; if found purus idiota, custody and profits may be granted by the king to a subject. Jurisprudence distinguishes natural idiots from persons non compos mentis since a particular time; some historical proposals existed to vest custody in relations with an equivalent settled on the crown. Special local customs may vest rights in manor lords for certain copyholders.
